Submicron magnetite-enhanced
tribromophenol removal and methanogenesis
under microaerobic condition
Fan Yang, Jing Wang,*
Chen Gu, Ying Han, Guang-fei Liu and Hong Lu
Abstract
BACKGROUND: To accelerate direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET), magnetite is supplemented in anaerobic activated
sludge (AS). However, it is usually reduced by dissimilatory iron reducing bacteria (DIRB). Therefore, an AS system supplemented
with submicron magnetite particles (Fe3O4/AS) in an up-ﬂow microaerobic sludge reactor was established, aiming to remove
tribromophenol (TBP) eﬃciently and alleviate the magnetite dissolution.
RESULTS: Under microaerobic condition (DO, 0.6 mg L−1), the eﬃciencies of removal of COD, TBP, and methane production
in Fe3O4/AS system were, respectively, 14.3%, 16.7%, and 27.2% higher than those of the AS system. Correspondingly,
the dehydrogenase (DHA) and Coenzyme F420 (CoF420) activities were separately 1.38-fold and 1.41-fold enhanced. The
enhanced biodegradation was via potential DIET, as visualized by microbes and magnetite particles, Geobacter enrichment and
c-type cytochromes (c-Cyts) increasement. Notably, magnetite majorly maintained an intact structure. In eﬄuents, the Fe(II)
concentrations were maintained at less than 10 mg L−1 under microaerobic conditions, far less than the amount under anaerobic
conditions, which might be due to the in situ redox cycle of Fe(III)-reduction and Fe(II)-reoxidation.
CONCLUSION: Signiﬁcant enhancements in removal eﬃciencies of TBP and COD and methanogenesis were demonstrated
in a Fe3O4/AS system, indicating intrinsically faster electron transfer via electrical conduction. Putative oxidation of dissolved
Fe(II) in situ occurred in microaerobic environments, which could protect magnetite in the system without extra magnetite
supplementation.

Keywords: direct interspecies electron transfer; methanogenesis; microaerobic; submicron magnetite; tribromophenol wastewater
INTRODUCTION
Tribromophenol (TBP) is widely used as a synthetic intermediate
of brominated ﬂame retardants (BFRs), pesticide, and the replace-
ment of pentachlorophenol in wood preservation. TBP has devel-
opmental neurotoxicity, embryotoxicity, and fetotoxicity eﬀects,
and this compound has been detected in various environmen-
tal matrices throughout the world, including marine and fresh
waters, sediments, soil, sewage sludge, and organisms.1–5 Notably,
wastewater containing TBP has attracted considerable concern
due to long-term residual and bioaccumulative properties, and the
developmentofeﬃcientandcost-eﬀectivetechniquestotreatTBP
wastewater is needed.
To date, limited physicochemical methods (phototransforma-
tion, chemical catalysis, etc.) have been reported to remove TBP,
while biodegradation is the eco-friendly and economical approach
for removal of TBP.6 However, TBP is resistant to aerobic biodegra-
dation due to the electron-withdrawing properties of bromine.
But anaerobic dehalogenation via dehalorespiration using halo-
genated compounds as terminal electron acceptors occurs more
easily.7 Previous studies have reported that both activated sludge
(AS) and pure strains exhibit anaerobic biodegradability of TBP.8,9
Lei et al. isolated Bacillus sp. GZT isolate, which was capable of
debrominating and mineralizing TBP, inferring that anaerobic
reductive debromination could act as the major degradation
pathway in the process of mineralizing TBP.10 However, the elec-
tron transfer rate is relatively low under anaerobic conditions,
which limits the rate of the dehalogenation process. To solve this
problem, diﬀerent mediators have been applied in biodegrada-
tion processes as electron shuttles to accelerate electron transfer,
such as vitamin B12 (VB12) and anthraquinone-2,6-disulfonate
(AQDS).11,12 Recently, it has been documented that nanoparticle
magnetite (Fe3O4) and other conductive minerals can promote
direct interspecies electron transfer (DIET) in a range of metabolic
processes, including a syntrophic metabolism between dehalo-
genating and non-dehalogenating bacteria under anaerobic

conditions.13–15 Moreover, it has been well demonstrated that
magnetite supplementation has beneﬁcial eﬀects on methano-
genesis and process stability by enhanced DIET.16
Nonetheless, it has been reported that the added magnetite
in AS systems could be reduced by dissimilatory iron reducing
bacteria (DIRB) under anaerobic conditions.17 Releasing biogenic
dissolved Fe(II) from magnetite (i.e. Fe(III)-reduction process),
may give rise to the undesirable loss and non-sustainability of
magnetite in wastewater treatment processes. To ﬁll such a knowl-
edge gap, the application of a microaerobic process may alleviate
the dissolution of magnetite by DIRB and conduct the potential
Fe(II)-reoxidation in the magnetite-supplemented AS system.
Besides, the microaerobic condition oﬀers apparent merits over
the conventional anaerobic process due to the high-eﬃciency of
hydrolysis, acidiﬁcation and complete degradation of the toxic
contaminants simultaneously.18–20
Hence, in order to promote the magnetite-mediated DIET as
well as restore the magnetite in situ, this study proposed that
submicron magnetite particles supplement the AS system at a
microaerobic dissolved oxygen (DO) level (0.3–1.0 mg L−1) to set
up a Fe3O4/AS system to treat TBP wastewater. The objectives of
this study were1 to elucidate the eﬀects of submicron magnetite
particles on TBP removal and methanogenesis under microaerobic
conditions2; to investigate whether or not the supplemented
magnetite is maintained in continuous culture under microaerobic
conditions;3 and to explore the underlying mechanisms in the
biodegradation process. This study can provide new possibilities
for high-rate TBP removal and biomethanation and help to cope
with the dissolution of magnetite in Fe3O4/AS systems.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
TBP and synthetic wastewater
TBP (98% purity) was purchased from Aladdin Reagent (Shang-
hai, China). A stock solution of TBP (5000 mg L−1) was pre-
pared in ethanol (99% purity) and stored at 4 ∘C in the dark
prior to use. The synthetic mineral medium was prepared in
deionized water and contained the following components (mg
L−1): NH4Cl (500), KH2PO4 (500), K2HPO4 (600), MgCl·6H2O (200),
CaCl2 (50), (NH4)2SO4 (100), and 1 mL L−1 of trace elements solu-
tions,whichcontainedH3BO3 (100),CuSO4·5H2O(58),ZnSO4·7H2O
(100), NiSO4·6H2O (112), MgSO4·7H2O (5000), FeSO4·7H2O (750),
MnSO4·H2O (188), and yeast (3000). Glucose as the carbon source
was added into the synthetic TBP wastewater to provide an initial
COD concentration of 1000 mg L−1. The pH value of the synthetic
TBP wastewater was adjusted to 7.0. The physicochemical char-
acteristics of the seed sludge (collected from the secondary clar-
iﬁer of the Chunliu River municipal wastewater treatment plant in
Dalian, China) are shown in Table S1, Supporting information.
Batch experiments
All batch experiments were conducted in the dark at room tem-
perature (20–25 ∘C) in serum ﬂasks (120 mL) which were supplied
with basic mineral medium (100 mL) and inoculated with acti-
vated sludge statically to achieve a ﬁnal mixed liquid suspended
solids (MLSS) of 330 mg L−1. Upon preparation, all bottles were
sealed with Teﬂon-faced butyl rubber stoppers and ﬂushed with
99.5% N2.

Additional batch experiments were also conducted to investi-

FeCl2). After 24 h of inoculation, the remaining COD contents were
detected and the methane production was measured by water dis-
placement method. All the tests were performed in duplicate in
darkness, in a constant temperature incubator at 35 ∘C.
The experimental set-up and operation
Two lab-scale microaerobic up-ﬂow sludge reactors were oper-
ated with a working volume of 1.35 L, namely R1 (AS, control)
and R2 (Fe3O4/AS), respectively. The initial MLSS in both reactors
were around 5000 mg L−1. The reactors were run in batch mode
during the ﬁrst 5 days for start-up and then switched to contin-
uous mode with daily feeding. R2 was supplemented with sub-
micron magnetite at a mass ratio of 0.25; R1 was not amended
(control). They were continuously fed with synthetic wastewa-
ter containing TBP at a controlled ﬂow rate using a peristaltic
pump with 50% volume exchange ratio and 1 cycle per day (HRT,
24 h). The inﬂuent was purged with 99.5% of N2 to maintain
DO below 0.05 mg L−1 and reﬂux bottles equipped with aera-
tion devices were used to maintain the microaerobic DO condi-
tion. Both reactors were maintained at pH ∼7 and the tempera-
ture was kept at 35 ∘C± 2 ∘C using a water bath throughout the
experiment. The schematic diagram of reactor conﬁguration is
shown in Fig. 1.
The operation of reactors was divided into three periods accord-
ing to the operating conditions. The time period and operating
conditions for each period are tabulated in Table 1. During the
operational period (Day 1–65), reactors were acclimated with the
increase of COD (1000–2000 mg L−1) and TBP (5–20 mg L−1) at
0.6 mg L−1 DO concentration. Anaerobic, microaerobic and aero-
bic conditions were introduced to evaluate the eﬀect on TBP and

Analytical methods
COD, MLSS, sludge volume index (SVI) were all determined accord-
ing to Standard Methods.21 DO and pH were measured using a
digital DO meter (YSI, Model 55, Yellow Springs, Ohio, USA) and
a digital pH meter (PHS-25, Leici Company, Shanghai, China).
TBP concentrations of inﬂuents and eﬄuents were determined
by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) (Shimadzu
LC-20AT, Kyoto, Japan) equipped with a DAD detector set at
286 nm as described in reference 22. Coenzyme F420 was tested
by the classic procedure of spectrophotometric study.23 A sample
of 2 mL from the reactor was ﬁrst disintegrated and suspended in
a Bead Bug (D 1030, Benchmark, Sayreville, New Jersey, USA) at
500 oscillations min−1 for 100 s, then centrifuged at 10 000 rpm
and 4∘C for 15 min to remove the waste debris. The suspensions
were measured using a ﬂuorescence/luminescence spectrometer
(LS 55, Perkin Elmer, Akron, Ohio, USA) under the synchronous
scan regime. The diﬀerence between excitation and emission
wavelengths was 20 nm. The excitation wavelength was changed
from 360 nm to 480 nm and the emission wavelength was syn-
chronously changed from 380 nm to 500 nm. Fluorescence at
420 nm was used in the experiments. Particle size of granules was
tested with a laser particle analyzer (Mastersizer 2000, Malvern,
Royston, England). The association of magnetite particles and bac-
terial cells on Day 65 was observed and photographed by a scan-
ning electron microscope (SEM) (NOVA NanoSEM 450, FEI, Oregon,
USA). The total dehydrogenase (DHA) activity was measured as
described by Feng et al.24 A ferrozine colorimetric method for Fe(II)
determination was performed using a UV–visible spectropho-
tometer (V-560, JASCO, Tokyo, Japan) at 560 nm. X-ray diﬀraction
(XRD) analysis was performed using a XRD-7000 diﬀractometer
(Shimadzu) with a Cu K𝛼radiation source. The extracellular poly-
meric substances (EPS) were extracted from the samples using
a heat technique.25 The total heme c contents and the heme c
contents in EPS were measured by the methods recorded by Berry
et al.26 The cytochrome peroxidase reaction was conducted on the
basis of the methods described by Yin et al. and the transmission
electron microscope (TEM) observation was performed according
to the methods described by Duan et al. using a Tecnai F30 TEM
(FEI).27,28 Biogas production was measured volumetrically using a
water displacement method at room temperature (25–30∘C).The
results were analyzed and compared using one-way ANOVA with
TUKEY’s test at the signiﬁcance level of 0.05.
16S rRNA amplicon sequencing and data processing
At the end of the microcosm incubation, sludge samples were col-
lected and stored at −80 ∘C until further analyses. Genomic DNA
was extracted using the FastDNA Spin Kit for Soil (MP Biomedi-
cal, Santa Ana, California, USA) following the protocols. 16S rRNA
genes were ampliﬁed using the bacterial universal primers (515F
and 806R) with speciﬁc barcode. All PCR reactions were carried
out in 30 μL reactions with 15 μL of Phusion® High-Fidelith PCR
Master Mix (New England Biolabs, Ipswich, Massachusetts, USA);
0.2 μmol L-1 forward and reverse primers, and ∼10 ng template
DNA. Thermal cycling consisted of initial denaturation at 98 ∘C
for 1 min, followed by 30 cycles of denaturation at 98 ∘C for 10 s,
annealing at 50 ∘C for 30 s, and elongation at 72 ∘C for 30 s. Finally,
72 ∘C for 5 min. PCR products were quantiﬁed, mixed, puriﬁed and
sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq platform at Novogene (Beijing,
China).
Paired-end reads from the DNA products were merged by using
FLASH.29 Paired-end reads were assigned to each sample accord-
ing to the unique barcode. Sequences were analyzed using QIIME
(Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology).30 Ambiguous N,
low-quality tags, chimers were ﬁltered to generate high quality
tags with default parameters. Sequences with similarity higher
than 97% were clustered into an Operational Taxonomic Unit
(OTU). Representative sequences were picked for each OTU and
annotated using the RDP classiﬁer.31 Perl scripts were used to
analyze the 𝛼-diversity indices. In order to compute 𝛼-diversity,
we rariﬁed the OTU table according to the sample with the least
sequences with the script in QIIME. The community richness and
𝛼-diversity were estimated by Observed species, Chao1, Shannon,
Simpson and ACE. Rarefaction curves were generated to compare
the level of bacterial OTU diversity.
RESULTS AND DISCUSSION
Tribromophenol removal performance
The COD removal eﬃciencies of the Fe3O4/AS system with diﬀer-
ent sizes of magnetite particles are shown in Figure S1, Supporting
information. The results showed that the AS + submicron-Fe3O4
system exhibited excellent COD removal eﬃciency (84.5%), com-
pared with AS + micron-Fe3O4 (80.2%) and AS + nano-Fe3O4
(78.3%). The submicron size had a much larger speciﬁc surface

enhance electrons transfer with microbes. Ma et al. reported that
the tiny particle structure of nanoscale material might penetrate
the microbial cell membrane, lead to inactivation and thus reduce
the capability of biodegradation.32 The lower toxicity of submicron
magnetite particles could contribute to better bioactivity of the
AS/Fe3O4 system. Therefore, submicron magnetite particles were
supplemented in the following reactor operations.
The removal eﬃciencies of COD and TBP in R1 and R2 are shown
in Fig. 2. The initial inﬂuent concentrations were COD = 1000 mg
L−1, TBP = 5 mg L−1, and the COD removal eﬃciency of R2 was
91.3% after 35 days of incubation, which was signiﬁcantly higher
than that of R1 (9.2%, P < 0.05). However, there was no remarkable
diﬀerence in terms of TBP removal eﬃciency (>95%) in both reac-
tors. The inﬂuent concentration was then altered to COD = 1500,
TBP = 10 mg L−1 at Day 35. The removal eﬃciencies of COD and
TBP in R2 were up to 81.0% and 89.6% at Day 50, which were 16.1%
and 14.4% higher than those of R1, respectively. Thus, the mediat-
ing eﬀect of the magnetite particles in R2 had an advantage over R1
during this period. Subsequently, the inﬂuent concentration was
enhanced to COD = 2000 mg L−1, TBP = 20 mg L−1 at Day 51 and
maintained for 25 days. The TBP removal eﬃciency of R2 was sig-
niﬁcantlyhigherthanthatofR1 (average13.9%,P < 0.05).Similarly,
the COD removal eﬃciency of R2 was signiﬁcantly higher than that
ofR1 (10.2%,P < 0.05).TheaboveresultsshowedthattheFe3O4/AS
system could cope with the higher inﬂuent loads of COD and TBP.
Sludge properties were measured to evaluate the stability of AS
and Fe3O4/AS systems, including granular particle size and SVI.
Figure 3. Sludge size distribution in both reactors during operation on day
24 (a) and on Day 60 (b).
As shown in Fig. 3, the average granular diameters in R2 were
approximately 0.123 and 1.833 mm on Day 24 and Day 60, respec-
tively, which were signiﬁcantly larger than those of R1 (0.084 and
1.370 mm). These data revealed that submicron magnetite par-
ticles could obviously accelerate the sludge granulation. Time
course proﬁles of SVI on day 1, 30, 45, and 65 are given in Table 2.
It was found that the granulation degree of sludge increased
with increasing reaction time. The SVI values of R2 were signiﬁ-
cantly lower than those of R1, indicating that the Fe3O4/AS system
exhibited a speciﬁc advantage of settleability over the AS system.
By comparison, the Fe3O4/AS system could observably shorten
the start-up process by promoting the formation of granular
sludge.
To investigate the impacts of diﬀerent DO concentrations on TBP
and COD removal, anaerobic, microaerobic and aerobic conditions
were employed for reactor operation. As shown in Fig. 4(a), the
highest TBP removal eﬃciency was 89.3% in the Fe3O4/AS sys-
tem at 0.11 mg L−1 of DO, signiﬁcantly higher than that of the AS
system (17.4%, P < 0.05). The enhanced TBP removal was proba-
bly due to the magnetite-mediated DIET with strong dehalogena-
tion performance under anaerobic conditions. However, the COD
removal eﬃciencies decreased to 68.1% and 80.6% in R1 and R2,
respectively,underanoxicconditions(Fig. 4(b)),owingtothelower
hydrolysis acidiﬁcation eﬃciency and biodegradable rate. Further-
more, as shown in Fig. 4(d), this process could not be sustainable
in long-term operation due to the dissolution of magnetite under
anaerobic conditions, consistent with previous reports.15,16

(90.1%) at 1.51 mg L−1 of DO in R2 (13.2% higher than that of
R1), whereas anaerobic methanogenesis and TBP removal were
inhibited. At 0.68 mg L−1 of DO, the removals of TBP and COD in

DIET, microaerobic conditions could provide the possibility of
recycling magnetite in situ without adding extra magnetite during
long-term operation.
Methanogenesis performance
Anaerobic digestion contained steps of hydrolysis, acidiﬁca-
tion, acetogenesis and methanogenesis. Of which, anaerobic
methanogenesis performance could be an indicator for complete
mineralization of organic compounds.33 To probe the eﬀects of
submicron magnetite on methanogenesis during the operational
period, methanogenesis performance was analyzed under diﬀer-
ent DO conditions. As shown in Fig. 4(c), methane production of
R2 exceeded that of R1 by 16.0%, 27.2%, and 21.6% under aerobic,
microaerobic, and anaerobic conditions, respectively, reaching
168, 216, and 223 mL day−1, respectively. These data indicated
that the Fe3O4/AS system had excellent methanogenic activity
under diﬀerent DO conditions. It was found that the methane
production in R2 under microaerobic conditions was remarkably
higher than the anaerobic methane production of R1, which might
likely result from the enhanced DIET and the supposed long-term
protection of magnetite by microaerobic conditions.

indicator of the activities of H2-utilizing methanogens.34 More-
over, Wang et al. showed that CoF420 was a H2 carrier in the

Microbial community analysis
A total of 138 818 clean tags (73 548 in R1 and 65 270 in R2) were
sequenced from two sludge samples collected from both reac-
tors and clustered to 1653 OTUs (1653 in R1 and 1624 in R2). Pro-
teobacteria, Spirochaetes, Bacteroidetes, Actinobacteria, Chloroﬂexi
and Firmicutes were the dominant phyla in sludge, accounting for
more than 80% of the total bacteria community. The presence
of Fe3O4 increased Proteobacteria and decreased Bacteroidetes
at the phylum level in R2 (Fig. 5(a)). The increase of Proteobac-
teria phylum was attributed to the enrichment of Geobacter at
genus level (Fig. 5(b)). Rarefaction curves in Figure S2 indicate
that there was no signiﬁcant diﬀerence in 𝛼-diversity between
magnetite-amended (R2) sample and control group (R1), which
was further demonstrated by Shannon, Simpson, Chao1, ACE and
goods-coverage indices.
To date, DIET of Geobacter co-cultures have been documented
in the processes of fumarate reduction, methane production,
and nitrate reduction.13,35,36 The syntrophic metabolism between
Geobacter and dehalorespiring microorganisms is a tentative
mechanism for DIET in the TBP debromination process, which can
enhance dehalorespiration by adding excessive electron donors
in bioremediation applications.15 The presence of magnetite
particles stimulated the growth of Geobacter species of Proteobac-
teria phylum in R2. In addition, the enriched Geobacter, implying
potential DIET, could explain the increased methane production
and TBP removal eﬃciency in R2. Hence, it could be presumed
that the enrichment of Geobacter species and their syntrophic
association with other bacteria (e.g. dehalorespiring bacteria and
methanogens) would accomplish reductive debromination and
methane production eﬀectively.
c-type cytochromes and dehydrogenase
It has been proposed that c-Cyt played important roles in facilitat-
ing electron transfer via DIET and was abundant in the periplasm
of Geobacter sp.37 For instance, G. metallireducens GS-15 had
evolved specialized mechanisms in the transfer electrons to G.
sulfurreducens PCA, the methanogenic archaea Methanosaeta
harundinacea via OmcS (a multihaem c-Cyt) and nanowires (pili,
an extracellular structure formed by protein ﬁlaments).38,39 Hemes,
as the electron transfer centers of c-Cyts, were detected as the
indirect reﬂection of c-Cyts contents. As shown in Table 3, the total
heme c contents and heme c contents in EPS in R2 were 1.59 ± 0.16
and 0.53 ± 0.03 mmol L-1 g−1 protein, which were approximately
23.6% and 22.6% higher than those in R1. The greater amount of
heme c in R2 manifested the higher c-Cyts level inside the Fe3O4/AS
system, implying possible stimulation in electron transfer rate.
In order to further investigate the variation of c-Cyts in
both reactors, the cytochrome reactive histochemical stain
3,3′-diaminobenzidine (DAB) was applied on Day 65. The region
of the cytochrome peroxidase stain of cells taken from R2 was
much greater than R1, consistent with more heme c contents,
indicating much faster enzymatic reaction engaged in the
magnetite-mediated DIET process. Moreover, the microbial cells

nanoparticles could function similarly to c-Cyts to facilitate shorter

the lack of c-Cyts and nanowires in conductivity enhancement.35
Aulenta et al. showed that the magnetite nanoparticles could
promote DIET from G. sulfurreducens PCA to Desulﬁtobacterium
spp. and Dehalococcoides spp. in a trichloroethene (TCE) reduc-
tive degradation process.15 Accordingly, we inferred that the
submicron magnetite particles, as the electron conduits, had
a substantial stimulatory eﬀect on TBP removal and methane
production by promoting potential DIET between Geobacter and
other functional bacteria.
As shown in Table 3, the DHA activity was greatly enhanced in
the presence of submicron magnetite particles in R2 and reached
18.59 ± 1.04 mg TF/ (L gMLSS h) on Day 65 (1.38-fold higher
than that of AS system). The microbial activity on organic matter
removal and electron transfer could be reﬂected by the total DHA
activity.40,41 Therefore, the increased DHA contents due to submi-
cron magnetite in R2 removed the contaminants more eﬀectively
and accelerated the electron transfer among cells.
Electrically conductive minerals such as magnetite particles
could serve as electron conduits in the proposed DIET mecha-
nism, which required an intimate association between magnetite
particles and microbial cells. Sludge samples were taken from
both reactors for morphological analysis on Day 65. In comparison
with R1 (Fig. 6(c)), the cells in R2 appeared tightly contacted
and the submicron magnetite crystals appeared as punctuated
particles evenly distributed and intimately associated with micro-
bial cells, with EPS attached to the cell surface (Fig. 6(d)). These
results indicated that the composite structure of Fe3O4/AS could
shorten the electron transfer distance between interspecies
consortia, potentially creating a network comprised of microor-
ganisms and conductive minerals, thus providing support of
a magnetite-mediated DIET mechanism. We propose that the
associated structure of magnetite with microbial consortia might
increase the abundance of Geobacter sp., c-Cyts contents, and DHA
activity, thus enhancing potential DIET sequentially and providing
more energy to syntrophic metabolism and pollutants removal.
Mineral phase analysis
To further explore whether the magnetite particles convert into
other forms of iron oxides, the Fe3O4/AS complex taken from R2
was subjected to XRD analysis (Fig. 7). Magnetite and goethite
were observed and identiﬁed with JCPDS Card No. 11-0614 and
JCPDS Card No. 03-0249 respectively, which indicated that the
added magnetite was partly transformed into goethite during
operation. Goethite, as a kind of semi-conductor, could enhance
anaerobic biodegradation and methanogenesis by assisting
DIET.42 Thus, both the added magnetite and the generated
goethite in the Fe3O4/AS system might have positive eﬀects
on DIET.

Role of dissolved Fe(II) on TBP biodegradation
and Methanogenesis
The dissolution of added magnetite was obtained by periodically
measuring the dissolved Fe(II) concentration in the eﬄuents
during reactor operation (Table 2). As shown in Fig. 2(d), it was
surprising that the microaerobic condition enabled the dissolved
Fe(II) to maintain a relatively low concentration (6.8 mg L−1 on
Day 65), which was far less than the amount under anaerobic
conditions (33.2 mg L−1 on Day 65). As mentioned above, DIRB
utilized Fe(III) as terminal electron acceptors for their growth
under anoxic conditions, which was assumed to result in the
increase of dissolved Fe(II) concentration.16 Hence, the microaero-
bic condition largely mitigated the consumption of magnetite by
DIRB and accelerated the biodegradation of organic contaminants
simultaneously, which might prolong the function time of the
added magnetite material in long-term operation.
To further investigate the eﬀects of diﬀerent concentrations of
dissolved Fe(II) on biodegradation, the results of batch experi-
ments are shown in Fig. S3. Compared with the control group
Xc (AS), X1 (AS +10 mg L−1 Fe(II)) and X2 (AS +20 mg L−1 Fe(II))
promoted COD removal and methane production to diﬀerent
degrees, indicating that the presence of Fe(II) enhanced the activ-
ity of anaerobic microorganisms. The COD removal eﬃciency and
the methane production in X1 system were 11.7% and 28.1%
higher than those of Xc, indicating that the relatively low concen-
tration of dissolved Fe(II) (<10 mg L−1) released in R2 reactor had a
profound inﬂuence on the biodegradation and methanogenesis,
which was consistent with Wang et al.33
CONCLUSIONS
It was demonstrated that remarkable enhancements in the
removal eﬃciencies of TBP and COD and methanogenesis through
adding submicron magnetite particles in activated sludge reac-
tors. The direct visualization of the association of magnetite
with microbes (SEM), the enrichment of Geobacter sp. and the
increased contents of c-Cyts in Fe3O4/AS system indicated the
potential magnetite-mediated DIET process, which provided
intrinsically faster electron transfer via electrical conduction and
thus achieved the excellent biodegradation performances. It was
found that putative oxidation of dissolved Fe(II) in situ occurred
in microaerobic environments and protected magnetite in the
Fe3O4/AS system without extra magnetite supplementation. The
ﬁndings of this study could provide possibility for the more eﬃ-
cient treatment of TBP wastewater by modiﬁed activated sludge
reactors.
